title: Structures, Senses and Survival
bigQuestion: How do the parts of a living thing help it stay alive, and what do fossils tell us about life that is gone?

story.title: The Fossil in the Mazon Creek Rock
story.kicker: A rust-colored lump from an old coal mine, a hammer tap, and a creature no one had ever seen.
paragraphs: South of Chicago, near the town of Braidwood, there are hills of gray and rust-colored rock. They are not natural hills. Machines piled them up when they dug for coal. Mixed into the piles are hard, rounded lumps called concretions. Most look like nothing. But some of them hold a secret. In 1955, a man named Francis Tully went walking there with a hammer.

Tully was a pipe fitter who hunted fossils on weekends. He picked up a lump and tapped it. It split along a hidden crack, like a book opening. Inside was the shape of an animal. It had a long, soft body, a thin neck ending in a claw with tiny teeth, and eyes on the ends of a stiff bar. Tully had never seen anything like it. Neither had anyone else.

He took it to the Field Museum in Chicago. The scientists were puzzled too. It was not a fish, not a worm, not a squid. They nicknamed it the Tully monster. In 1966, it got a scientific name: Tullimonstrum. Thousands more have been found since. Every one comes from this one small area in Illinois. In 1989, Illinois made it the state fossil.

The rock told a story too. About 300 million years ago, this part of Illinois sat near the equator. Rivers ran through a steamy swamp forest into a shallow sea. Ferns as tall as trees dropped their leaves in the mud. Jellyfish, shrimp, worms and Tully monsters lived in the water. When they died, mud buried them fast, and the mud slowly hardened into rock around them.

Today that swamp forest is an old coal mine, and part of the mine has filled with water. The ferns became coal. The mud became stone. The animals became fossils. Scientists still argue about what the Tully monster really was. But the fossil proves one thing for sure: the living things of Illinois, and the place itself, have changed almost beyond imagining.
story.think: The Tully monster's eyes sat on the ends of a stiff bar. What might that structure have been good for? How could you test your idea?

lessons.title: A Plant's Outside Parts
lessons.mainIdea: Roots, stems, leaves, flowers and thorns are external structures, and each one does a job that helps the plant survive, grow and reproduce.
reading: Pull a dandelion out of a sidewalk crack. Look at what comes up. A long, tough root went deep for water. A hollow stem held the leaves up toward light. Flat leaves caught sunlight to make food. A yellow flower made seeds. Each part is a *structure*, a part with a shape and a job.

Plants have parts for defense too. A rose has *thorns*, so deer think twice before biting. A cactus has spines and a thick waxy skin to keep water in. Some leaves are hairy or bitter. Milkweed leaks a sticky white sap that gums up the mouths of most insects. Monarch caterpillars are among the few that can handle it.

Structures help plants reproduce, too. Bright petals and sweet nectar bring bees. Bees carry *pollen* from flower to flower. A maple seed has a wing so it spins away from the parent tree. A burr has hooks that grab a passing dog's fur. Each structure solves a problem the plant cannot walk away from.

words.d: a part of a living thing that has a shape and a job
sharp points on a plant's stem that keep animals from eating it
a fine powder from flowers that must reach another flower for seeds to form

look.title: Two Plants in the Same Yard
look.text: A prairie plant called compass plant grows on the school prairie. Its root goes down about 3 meters, deeper than a basement. Next to it, a lawn grass has roots only a few centimeters deep. In August it has not rained for three weeks. The grass is brown and crunchy. The compass plant is still green.
look.prompt: Which root structure gave an advantage in the dry August? What might happen to each plant if the summer were wet instead?

check.q: What is the main job of a plant's roots?
choices: To take in water and hold the plant in place
check.why: Roots reach into the soil for water and anchor the plant. Leaves catch light, and flowers make seeds.

check.q: Why does a rose have thorns?
choices: To keep animals from eating it
check.why: Thorns are a defense structure. They make deer and other animals think twice before biting.

check.q: A maple seed has a thin wing. What problem does it solve?
choices: Getting the seed away from the parent tree
check.why: The wing makes the seed spin and drift, so it lands away from the parent and does not compete with it.

lessons.title: An Animal's Outside Parts
lessons.mainIdea: Shells, fur, feathers, claws, beaks and skin are external structures that protect animals and help them move, eat and stay warm.
reading: A painted turtle *basks* on a log in a Chicago lagoon. When a shadow passes, it slides into the water. Its shell is a bone box that a raccoon cannot bite through. Its *webbed* feet push it fast through water. Its eyes sit high on its head so it can see while nearly hidden. Every outside part has a job.

Animals that live through Illinois winters have parts for the cold. A white-tailed deer grows a thick, hollow-haired coat in fall. A chickadee fluffs its feathers to trap warm air. A frog cannot do either. It rests at the bottom of a pond and waits. Its skin is thin so it can take in oxygen from the water.

Parts for eating are easy to spot. A hawk has hooked *talons* to grab and a hooked beak to tear. A beaver has orange front teeth that never stop growing, so it can chew wood all its life. A mosquito has a needle mouth. Look at an animal's outside parts and you can often guess how it lives.

words.d: rests in the sun to warm up
having skin stretched between the toes, which helps push against water
the sharp, curved claws of a bird of prey such as a hawk

look.title: The Mystery Skull
look.text: A student finds a small skull in the woods near the Des Plaines River. It has long, sharp front teeth on top and bottom. The teeth at the back are pointed too, not flat. The eye holes face forward. The skull is about as long as your hand.
look.prompt: What might this animal have eaten? Which structures are your evidence?

check.q: What is a turtle's shell for?
choices: Protection from animals that would bite it
check.why: The shell is a bone box. A raccoon or other animal cannot bite through it.

check.q: Why do a beaver's front teeth keep growing?
choices: So it can chew wood its whole life without wearing them away
check.why: Chewing wood wears teeth down. Teeth that keep growing let the beaver keep chewing all its life.

check.q: A chickadee fluffs its feathers in January. What is it doing?
choices: Trapping warm air near its body
check.why: Fluffed feathers hold a layer of warm air against the skin, like a puffy coat.

lessons.title: Parts on the Inside
lessons.mainIdea: Internal structures, the heart, lungs, stomach, bones and brain, work together to keep an animal alive and growing.
reading: Press two fingers to the side of your neck. Feel the beat? That is your *heart*, a fist-sized pump. It pushes blood through tubes to every part of you. Blood carries oxygen and food to your body and carries waste away. A fish has a heart. So does a frog, a hawk and a mouse.

Take a deep breath. Your *lungs* filled with air. Oxygen from the air passes into your blood. A fish has no lungs. It pulls oxygen from water with its gills. Insects have no lungs either. They breathe through tiny holes along their sides. Different structures, same job: get oxygen in.

Your *skeleton* holds you up and guards what is soft. Ribs cage the heart and lungs. The skull is a helmet for the brain. A grasshopper wears its skeleton on the outside, like armor, and must shed it to grow. Your stomach breaks food into pieces small enough to use. Every inside part has a job, and the parts depend on each other.

words.d: the muscle that pumps blood through the body
the organs that take oxygen from the air into the blood
the bones that hold up a body and protect its soft parts

look.title: Resting Heartbeats Per Minute
look.prompt: What pattern do you see between an animal's size and its heart rate? How many times does a mouse heart beat while yours beats once?

check.q: What does the heart do?
check.why: The heart is a pump. It pushes blood, which carries oxygen and food, to every part of the body.

check.q: Fish have no lungs. How do they get oxygen?
choices: Through gills that pull oxygen from water
By coming up to breathe air every minute
check.why: Gills take oxygen out of water. Fish do the same job as lungs with a different structure.

check.q: Using the data, which is true?
choices: Bigger animals tend to have faster hearts
All animals have the same heart rate
Smaller animals tend to have faster hearts
check.why: The elephant's heart beats about 30 times a minute and the mouse's about 550. Smaller animals have faster hearts.

lessons.title: How the Eye Uses Light
lessons.mainIdea: We see because light bounces off objects, enters the eye through the pupil, and forms an image that the eye sends to the brain.
reading: Turn off every light in a closet. You see nothing. Not because your eyes are broken, but because there is no light. Seeing needs light. Light from the sun or a lamp bounces, or *reflects*, off things. Some of that bounced light enters your eye. A red apple reflects red light to your eye. That is why it looks red.

Light enters through the *pupil*, the black hole in the middle of the eye. In dim light the pupil opens wide to let more light in. In bright sun it shrinks. Behind it sits a clear lens. The lens bends the light into a sharp, upside-down picture on the *retina* at the back of the eye. The retina is a screen packed with cells that react to light.

The retina changes light into signals. A thick nerve carries the signals to the brain. The brain turns the signals into what you see, and flips the picture right side up. Animals' eyes fit their lives. An owl's huge eyes gather dim light. A rabbit's eyes sit on the sides of its head, so it can watch for a fox almost all the way around.

words.d: bounces off; light reflects off objects and into our eyes
the dark opening in the middle of the eye that lets light in
the layer at the back of the eye that turns light into signals for the brain

look.title: Darwin Looks at the Eye
look.text: In 1859 Darwin wrote that it might seem absurd to think the eye, with its ways of adjusting focus, letting in different amounts of light and correcting for blur, could have formed step by step. But he added that if many small, useful steps could be shown, from a simple light-sensing spot up to a complex eye, the idea should not be called impossible.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, 1859, chapter 6 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Darwin lists three things the eye can do. Which of them did you read about in this lesson?

check.q: Why can you not see in a completely dark closet?
choices: Your eyes shut down in the dark
There is no light to reflect off objects into your eyes
The retina only works in sunlight
The pupil closes all the way
check.why: Seeing needs light that bounces off objects and enters the eye. With no light, nothing reaches the retina.

check.q: What does the pupil do in dim light?
choices: Opens wider to let in more light
check.why: The pupil opens wide in dim light so more of the little light there is can get in.

check.q: A rabbit's eyes are on the sides of its head. What is the advantage?
choices: It can see almost all the way around for predators
It can see in total darkness
It can focus on tiny seeds
check.why: Side-facing eyes give a very wide view, so a rabbit can spot a fox coming from almost any direction.

lessons.title: Messages to the Brain
lessons.mainIdea: Eyes, ears, skin, nose and tongue send information to the brain through nerves, and the brain uses it to decide what the body does next.
reading: A ball flies toward your face. Your hands come up before you have time to think. How? Your eyes sent a message to your brain along *nerves*, thin threads that carry signals. Your brain sent a message back down other nerves to your arm muscles. The whole trip took a fraction of a second.

Every *sense* works this way. Ears catch sound and turn it into signals. Skin has tiny *sensors* for touch, heat, cold and pain. The nose and tongue sense chemicals in air and food. All of the signals travel to the brain. The brain sorts them and decides. Loud bang? Jump. Smell of smoke? Look for fire. Hot pan? Let go.

Other animals lean on different senses. A dog's nose has far more smell sensors than yours. A bat sends out high squeaks and listens for the echoes to find moths in the dark. A catfish tastes with its whole skin. Each animal's senses fit how it gets food and stays safe. But a sense is only useful if its message reaches the brain.

words.d: thin threads in the body that carry signals to and from the brain
a way of taking in information: sight, hearing, touch, smell or taste
tiny parts that notice one kind of thing, such as heat or pressure, and send a signal

look.title: The Drum Bench Test
look.text: Two students sit at the site's drum bench. One wears a blindfold. The other taps a drum on the left, then the right, then far away. Every time, the blindfolded student points toward the sound, then says how loud it was. Then they try it with one ear covered. The pointing gets less accurate.
look.prompt: What information did the ears send to the brain? Why did covering one ear make pointing harder?

check.q: What carries messages from your eyes to your brain?
check.why: Nerves are thin threads that carry signals from the senses to the brain and from the brain to the muscles.

check.q: You smell smoke and go look for a fire. Put the steps in order.
choices: Brain decides, nose senses, body moves
Body moves, nose senses, brain decides
Nose senses, body moves, brain decides
Nose senses, brain decides, body moves
check.why: The sense comes first, the signal goes to the brain, the brain decides, and then the body acts.

check.q: How does a bat find a moth in the dark?
choices: By listening for echoes of its own squeaks
check.why: A bat sends out high squeaks and hears them bounce back off the moth. Its ears do the job eyes cannot in the dark.

lessons.title: The Brain Decides
lessons.mainIdea: The brain uses information from the senses, plus memory, to respond quickly and to learn from what happened before.
reading: A friend holds a ruler so it hangs just above your open fingers. Without warning, she drops it. You pinch. The ruler slides 15 centimeters before you catch it. That means it took about 0.17 seconds for your eyes to see it move, your brain to decide, and your fingers to close. That is your *reaction time*.

Try it ten times. Most people get a little faster. That is not because their nerves changed. It is because the brain learned. It stored a *memory* of the drop and got ready. Memory turns one experience into a better response next time. A squirrel that was chased by a hawk near the oak stays away from the oak.

The brain also decides what to ignore. Right now your skin feels your socks. Your brain is not bothering you about it. But if a spider crawled across your ankle, you would notice instantly. Sorting important signals from unimportant ones is one of the brain's biggest jobs. Animals that sort well tend to survive.

words.d: the time between noticing something and responding to it
information the brain stores from past experience

look.title: The Ruler Drop Test
look.cite: calculated from how falling objects speed up (free fall), rounded
look.prompt: A student catches the ruler at 20 cm the first try and at 10 cm the tenth try. What changed, and about how much time did she gain?

check.q: What is reaction time?
choices: The time between seeing something and responding to it
The time it takes to fall asleep
check.why: Reaction time is the gap between noticing something, like the ruler moving, and doing something about it.

check.q: Using the data, catching the ruler at 30 cm means a reaction time of about:
check.why: The table shows 30 cm matches about 0.25 seconds, a quarter of a second.

check.q: Why do people usually get faster after several tries of the ruler test?
choices: The brain remembers and gets ready
check.why: The brain stores a memory of the drop and prepares, so it responds a little sooner each time.

lessons.title: Living in a Group
lessons.mainIdea: Living in a group helps some animals get food, stay safe and raise young better than they could alone.
reading: In October, Canada geese fly over Chicago in a V. The goose in front breaks the air. The ones behind ride the smoother air and save energy. When the leader tires, another takes its place. Geese honk to keep in touch. A single goose would tire faster and have no one to watch for danger. The *flock* is a survival tool.

Wolves hunt in a *pack*. One wolf cannot bring down an elk. Six can. Prairie dogs live in towns with lookouts. When one spots a hawk, it barks, and everyone dives underground. Honeybees split the work. Some guard, some gather, some feed the young. Prairie dog towns and bee hives are kinds of *colonies*. A hive of thousands can do what no single bee could.

Groups have costs too. Food must be shared. Sickness spreads faster. So not every animal lives in a group. A bobcat hunts alone. Still, for many animals, the group means more eyes, more warmth and more help. Bison on an Illinois prairie stand shoulder to shoulder in a blizzard, sharing heat.

words.d: a group of birds that live or travel together
a group of animals, such as wolves, that hunt together
groups of animals of one kind that live together in one place, such as bees in a hive

look.title: Musk Oxen in a Ring
look.text: In the far north, a pack of wolves circles a herd of musk oxen. The oxen do not run. The adults turn to face outward and form a tight ring, horns out. The calves stand in the middle. The wolves pace, test, and finally leave. A lone musk ox, caught away from the herd, does not have this option.
look.prompt: How does the ring help the calves? What does the lone musk ox lose by being alone?

check.q: Why do geese fly in a V?
choices: Because the leader is the oldest
The birds behind save energy in the leader's smoother air
check.why: The front goose breaks the air, and the geese behind ride smoother air. They take turns leading.

check.q: What does a prairie dog lookout do?
choices: Warns the others when a predator comes
check.why: The lookout barks when it spots a hawk or coyote, and the whole town dives underground.

check.q: Which is a cost of living in a group?
check.why: Living close together means a sickness can pass quickly from one animal to the next. The others are benefits.

lessons.title: When the Pond Dries Up
lessons.mainIdea: When an environment changes, some living things survive in place, some move to a new place, and some die.
reading: A summer with almost no rain. By August, a pond near Springfield is a cracked mud flat. What happens to the living things? The answer is not the same for all of them. Some *survive* right there. Some move. Some die. Scientists watch which is which, and why.

Frogs with strong legs hop to a creek half a mile away. They move. Turtles dig into the damp mud below the surface and wait. They survive in place. Tadpoles cannot leave and cannot wait. They die. Cattail seeds sit in the dry mud, alive but not growing, ready for rain. The trait that matters is whichever one fits the new *conditions*.

Big changes have happened in Illinois before. Two hundred years ago, tall grass *prairie* covered most of the state. Then farms replaced almost all of it. Prairie chickens, which need wide grassland, nearly vanished. White-tailed deer, which like the edges of fields, are now everywhere. A change that hurts one kind can help another.

words.d: to stay alive through a hard time
the state of the environment: how wet, hot, cold or crowded a place is
a wide grassland with few trees; most of Illinois was prairie before farms

look.title: The Pond Count
look.text: A class counted living things at the pond in June and again in September, after the drought. June: 200 tadpoles, 30 frogs, 8 turtles, 50 dragonflies. September: 0 tadpoles, 3 frogs, 6 turtles, 2 dragonflies. A creek half a mile away had many more frogs in September than in June.
look.prompt: For each kind of animal, decide: did most survive in place, move, or die? What is your evidence?

check.q: The pond dries up. Which is the most likely outcome for a tadpole?
choices: It digs into mud and waits
check.why: A tadpole has no legs to leave and cannot wait in dry mud. Without water, it dies.

check.q: What are the three things that can happen to living things when the environment changes?
check.why: Some survive in place, some move to a new place, and some die. Which one depends on their traits.

check.q: Farms replaced Illinois prairie. Which sentence is true?
choices: Some kinds were harmed and some were helped
check.why: Prairie chickens nearly vanished, but white-tailed deer did well along the field edges.

lessons.title: How a Fossil Forms
lessons.mainIdea: A fossil is the preserved remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, usually formed when it was buried quickly in mud or sand.
reading: Most dead things vanish. A fish dies in a river and other animals eat it. Bacteria finish the job. Even the bones crumble. But once in a while, a dead thing is buried quickly, by a flood of mud or a slide of sand. Under the mud, there is little oxygen. Rot slows to a crawl. This is how a *fossil* begins.

Over thousands of years, more layers pile on top. The mud is squeezed into rock. Water seeping through carries dissolved *minerals*. The minerals slowly replace the bone or shell, or fill the hollow it left behind. What remains is a copy in stone. Fossils can also be traces: a footprint, a burrow, a leaf print. These are *trace fossils*.

In 1669, a Danish doctor named Nicolas Steno made a simple claim. Rock layers form one on top of another, so the bottom layer is oldest. And the shark-tooth-shaped stones in the rocks were exactly that: sharks' teeth, turned to stone. Fossils were not strange rocks. They were once alive. Every fossil is a life that the earth kept a record of.

words.d: the remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, preserved in rock
hard, nonliving materials in rock and water that can slowly replace bone or shell
fossils of something a living thing did, like a footprint or burrow, not of its body

look.title: Steno Reads the Layers
look.text: In 1669 Steno wrote that when a layer of sediment was being laid down, the layer beneath it must already have been solid, so lower layers are older than the layers above them. He also argued that objects found inside rock, such as shells and sharks' teeth, were placed there when the rock was still soft mud, and that they had once been the parts of living animals.
look.prompt: If you find a fish fossil in a layer below a fern fossil, which is older? How do you know?

check.q: Why does quick burial help form a fossil?
choices: Under mud there is little oxygen, so rot slows down
check.why: Buried under mud, the body is away from scavengers and oxygen, so it can last long enough to be replaced by minerals.

check.q: Which is a trace fossil?
check.why: A trace fossil records something an animal did, like walking. The others are parts of a body.

check.q: Steno said the bottom rock layer is usually the oldest. Why?
choices: Because layers form one on top of another over time
check.why: Each new layer settles on top of the last. So the deeper you go, the older the layer.

lessons.title: Inside the Mazon Creek Concretions
lessons.mainIdea: Mazon Creek fossils near Braidwood, Illinois, are unusually complete because soft-bodied animals were buried fast in mud that hardened around them.
reading: Most fossils are hard parts: bones, shells, teeth. Soft parts rot before they can be buried. That makes Mazon Creek special. Its rocks hold jellyfish, worms, shrimp, insects, and the Tully monster, soft bodies and all. Collectors find these *soft-bodied* animals inside rounded rust-colored lumps called *concretions*. Split one and it may open like a book.

Why here? About 300 million years ago, rivers poured mud into a shallow sea. Storms and floods buried animals and plants in minutes. Iron in the water hardened the mud around each body into a shell of stone before it could rot. The rest of the mud stayed soft and later washed away or became coal.

Coal mining brought the concretions to the surface. For years, collectors walked the *spoil piles* after rain, when wet rocks showed their cracks. Some soak the lumps in water and freeze them, over and over, until they split. Many of the best finds went to the Field Museum in Chicago. You can see a Tully monster there today.

words.d: having no bones or hard shell, like a jellyfish or a worm
hard, rounded lumps of rock that formed around something buried in mud
the heaps of rock and dirt a mine digs out and leaves behind

look.title: A Scientist Describes the Tully Monster
look.text: In 1966, Field Museum scientist Eugene Richardson described the new animal in the journal Science. He reported that it had a long body, a narrow front end like a neck that ended in a claw-shaped jaw with small teeth, and a stiff bar across the body with an eye at each end. He wrote that he could not place it in any known group of animals.
look.prompt: Richardson listed the parts he could see, but said he could not tell what group the animal belonged to. Why is it good science to say 'I do not know'?

check.q: Why are soft-bodied fossils so rare in most places?
choices: Soft animals never existed long ago
Soft parts rot before they can be buried
Soft animals live only in deserts
check.why: Soft bodies rot fast. Only quick burial and fast-hardening mud, as at Mazon Creek, can save them.

check.q: What is a concretion?
choices: A hard, rounded lump of rock that may hold a fossil
check.why: A concretion is a lump of rock that hardened around something buried in mud. Split open, it may show a fossil.

check.q: What happened to the Mazon Creek animals right after they died?
choices: They floated in the sea for years
Floods buried them in mud very quickly
check.why: Storms and floods buried them in minutes, and iron in the water hardened the mud before they could rot.

lessons.title: What Fossils Tell Us
lessons.mainIdea: By comparing fossils with living things and with the rocks around them, scientists learn what lived long ago and how the environment has changed.
reading: Illinois has no ocean. Yet *limestone* all over the state is packed with fossil sea creatures: corals, sea lilies, clam-like shells. Pick up a chunk of gravel and you may hold one. The only explanation is that a shallow sea once covered Illinois. The rocks are the evidence. Scientists *infer* the past from clues, the way a detective does.

Fossils also show what a place was like. Fern fossils from Mazon Creek match ferns that grow today only in hot, wet places. So Illinois was once hot and wet. Mammoth bones found in Illinois gravel pits show an ice-age world of cold grassland. Same ground, three different worlds: sea, swamp, ice.

Fossils show living things that are gone, too. No Tully monster swims anywhere today. No mammoth walks. Scientists say these kinds are *extinct*. Comparing an extinct animal's structures with living animals gives clues. A sharp, claw-like mouth means a hunter. Big eyes mean it found food by sight. Fossils let us ask questions about a world we can never visit.

words.d: a rock made mostly from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures
to figure out something you cannot see directly, using clues
no longer alive anywhere on Earth

look.title: Three Rocks From One Road Cut
look.text: Along a highway in central Illinois, a class studies a cliff of rock layers. Bottom layer: gray limestone full of fossil corals and shells. Middle layer: dark shale with fern prints and a thin seam of coal. Top layer: loose gravel and sand with no fossils, dropped by a glacier.
look.prompt: Put the three worlds in order from oldest to newest. What was Illinois like in each one?

check.q: Illinois has fossil corals but no ocean. What do scientists infer?
choices: A shallow sea once covered Illinois
Someone brought the fossils from Florida
check.why: Corals live in the sea. Finding them in Illinois rock means a sea was once here.

check.q: What does 'extinct' mean?
choices: No longer alive anywhere on Earth
check.why: An extinct kind of living thing has no living members left anywhere.

check.q: Fern fossils in Illinois match ferns that live in hot, wet places today. What can you infer?
choices: Illinois was once hot and wet
The ferns were planted by people
check.why: If the fossil ferns are like ferns that need hot, wet places, Illinois was probably hot and wet when they grew.

review.why: Lungs are inside the body. Thorns, fur and a shell are on the outside.

review.q: How does light let you see a red apple?
choices: The apple makes its own light
Light reflects off the apple into your eye
Your eye sends light to the apple
Red apples glow in the dark
review.why: Light from a lamp or the sun bounces off the apple. Some of it enters your eye and reaches the retina.

review.q: What is the job of nerves?
choices: To carry signals between the senses and the brain
review.why: Nerves are the threads that carry signals from the senses to the brain and from the brain to the muscles.

review.q: Which is a way living in a group helps wolves?
choices: Together they can catch prey too big for one wolf
They do not need to eat
review.why: One wolf cannot bring down an elk, but a pack can.

review.q: A forest burns down. What could happen to the animals that lived there?
choices: Some survive, some move, some die
review.why: When an environment changes, the outcome depends on each animal's traits: some survive in place, some move, some die.

review.q: Why are Mazon Creek fossils special?
choices: They are the oldest fossils on Earth
They show soft-bodied animals, which rarely become fossils
review.why: Fast burial and quick-hardening mud saved jellyfish, worms and the Tully monster, soft bodies and all.

review.q: Steno said rock layers form one on top of another. So a fossil in a lower layer is:
choices: The same age as one above it
review.why: Lower layers were laid down first, so a fossil in a lower layer is older.

review.q: A cactus has spines and a waxy skin. What problem do these structures solve?
choices: Keeping water in and animals away
review.why: The waxy skin holds water in, and the spines keep thirsty animals from biting.
